claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys exhibit inherently sluggish bulk atomic diffusion at high temperature.
Suppressed bulk atomic diffusion limits elemental segregation.
Limiting elemental segregation stabilizes the alloy phase.
Suppressed bulk diffusion is the primary source of structural and chemical stability, rather than surface-oxidation effects.
A high-purity inert atmosphere produces minimal surface oxidation during the heat treatment.
Any additional instability observed in the oxidizing atmosphere would be attributable to oxidation rather than intrinsic diffusion.
Inert-treated samples will show less elemental segregation than oxidizing-atmosphere-treated samples.
Inert-treated samples will show less surface oxidation than oxidizing-atmosphere-treated samples.
Inert-treated samples will retain phase homogeneity and undergo minimal structural change relative to the as-synthesized baseline.
Oxidizing-atmosphere-treated samples will form more surface oxide than the as-synthesized baseline.
Oxidizing treatment may promote elemental segregation at grain boundaries or surfaces.
Both diffusion kinetics and oxidation processes are active in the proposed 800–1000°C range.
Oxygen partial pressure and temperature can strongly affect the stability and form of high-entropy oxides.
High-entropy materials can possess elevated high-temperature phase stability because configurational entropy lowers Gibbs free energy.
The prediction is restricted to temperatures below complete melting or loss of metastability.
The relative roles of diffusion and oxidation may vary with composition, treatment duration, temperature, and oxygen partial pressure.
Similar or greater segregation, phase instability, or surface degradation in the inert-treated sample than in the oxidized sample is designated as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies diffusion suppression, rather than oxidation, as the dominant stabilizer, but the comparison varies only oxygen availability and treats improved stability when oxidation is suppressed as necessary evidence. Such an atmosphere-dependent result primarily diagnoses an oxidation effect and does not independently establish that diffusion is dominant.

The mechanism says inert treatment isolates intrinsic diffusion, whereas the falsification rule rejects the diffusion-dominance hypothesis if oxidation suppression does not correlate with improved stability. A diffusion-dominant mechanism does not logically require that correlation.
